item.passage:
Lena Marsh had been drum major of the Corliss High marching band for nine days, and for nine days the back of the band had been late. From her ladder at the front of the formation she could hear it plainly: the trumpets nearest her hit each note on her beat, and the tubas forty yards behind them landed a hair after it, so that every chord arrived twice, once sharp and once smeared.

Mr. Dale, the director, watched from the top of the bleachers with his arms folded. On her first day he had told her that a drum major's job was to keep time. On her third, when she climbed up to ask what she was doing wrong, he had said, "You'll hear it," and that was all. Lena kept time. She had practiced against a metronome every night until her shoulders ached, and her right hand came down on the beat as cleanly as a clock's.

So on Thursday she turned around on the ladder and called to the back row. "You're dragging! Listen to the trumpets and stay with them."

The tubas tried. They listened harder, and the run-through went worse. Now the whole back half of the field was waiting for a sound to reach it before it played, and Lena could feel the music sliding out from under her hand like a rug.

Afterward, while the band packed up, the senior tuba player, a tall girl named Cass Ferreira, climbed the ladder's first two rungs and blew a strand of hair off her forehead. "We are listening," she said, leaning hard on the second word. "That's the trouble. By the time the trumpets reach us, they've already moved on."

Lena had never thought of the field as a distance. She had been treating forty yards of grass like a room. Sound needed time to cross it, only about a tenth of a second, but a tenth of a second was enough to blur a chord, and the tubas had been adding it on top of the time it took them to hear and respond.

On Friday she stayed facing forward. Before the run-through she climbed down, walked the length of the formation to the back row, and told the tubas to stop listening for the front. "Watch my hand," she said. "When it hits the bottom, play. Even if it sounds wrong to you."

It did sound wrong, Cass told her later. From the back row the trumpets now seemed to come in late, and the pull to wait for them was hard to fight. But from the top of the bleachers, where Mr. Dale stood, the chords landed closer together than they had all week.

He came down to the field when it was over. He looked at Lena, then at the back row, and said only, "Again, from the top." She climbed the ladder and raised her hand, and at the far end of the formation the whole back row was already watching it.

By supper the cold had held for eleven days,
the kind that makes the porch boards crack like knuckles
and freezes the hairs inside your nose.
My father had gone out at noon to start the truck
and let it run, just to keep it willing.

Then, low over the mountains to the west,
a band of clear sky opened under the cloud,
straight-edged, as if someone had lifted the lid
of the whole gray day an inch to look in.
My grandmother saw it from the sink
and said one word, and dried her hands.

By nine the wind arrived. It did not howl.
It leaned on the house the way a big dog leans,
warm through the window glass, and all night
the eaves let go of their icicles one by one,
a sound like someone setting down spoons.

In the morning the thermometer by the door
had climbed from below zero to past fifty.
The drifts along the fence had slumped
to gray crusts full of holes, and the yard
was a map of brown islands. My brother
went to school in his shirtsleeves, carrying his coat
like something a stranger had asked him to hold.

Snow eater, my grandmother called it,
the name her father used when the wind came
down off the rock in winter and took
the snow in a day and left the creek
running loud under the ice.

She opened every window in the house an inch.
She hung the rugs over the line. She said
it would not last, and set out the boots
by the door where we would find them,
and stood a while on the step in the soft air
with her arms crossed, watching the west
for the gray line that would bring the cold back.

The summer I was eleven, my family moved from an apartment in the city to Ardley, a river town of about four thousand people, where my mother had taken a job at the county hospital. In the city I had found my way by street signs and numbered avenues. Ardley had street signs too, but nobody used them.

I learned this my first week, when I asked a woman at the post office how to get to the public pool. She told me to go down past where the Starlite used to be, turn left at the old Kimble place, and keep on until I saw the field where they held the fair before it moved. I thanked her and walked for an hour. There was no Starlite. The old Kimble place, I learned much later, had burned in 1961.

My father, who sold insurance and so spent his days hunting for other people's houses, bought a county map and drew on it in pencil. Whenever someone gave him directions, he wrote the vanished places in where they had stood: the Starlite drive-in, the Kimble house, a feed store, a school torn down before he was born. By spring the map was gray with buildings that no longer existed.

It took me longer to understand what the directions were for. A person who gave them was telling you how long she had lived there. To follow them, you had to ask someone else, who would tell you that the Kimble place was the lot with two chimneys standing in it, and then who the Kimbles had been, and whom their daughter had married, and that the daughter's son now ran the hardware store. Every set of directions was a small history of the town, and an invitation to come back and ask for more.

I was slow to accept any of this. I wanted the town to be legible the way the city had been, all at once and to anyone. In my first winter I drew a map of Ardley for a school project, with every street name lettered in neat capitals, and I was stung when my teacher, who had grown up two streets from the school, praised it and then asked, kindly, why I had left off the swimming hole. I had no idea there was one.

We stayed in Ardley nine years. Near the end of them, a family moved into the house across the street, and their boy, about the age I had been, stopped me on the sidewalk to ask the way to the library. I meant to tell him to go two blocks to Fourth Street and turn right. What came out was, "Go down past where the bakery used to be." The bakery had closed that spring. He looked at me the way I must have looked at the woman in the post office, and I walked him there.

An artichoke defeats every shortcut. A knife is useless on it, and a fork is worse. You pull off one leaf at a time, dip its pale base in butter or lemon, draw it between your teeth to scrape off a thumbnail of soft flesh, and drop the rest on a plate that fills, as the meal goes on, with a heap of what you have left behind.

The artichoke is the bud of a thistle, picked before it can flower, and its defenses are still in place. In many varieties the outer leaves are tough and end in a small thorn. Toward the center they thin and soften and pale to yellow-green, until you reach a cone of leaves so thin you can eat them whole. Beneath that waits the choke, a mat of fine bristles that has to be scraped away with a spoon, and beneath the choke, at last, the heart, which is what people mean when they say they love artichokes.

What I love about the artichoke, though, is the twenty minutes it takes to get there. It will be eaten slowly or not at all, and it refuses to be eaten on the side of anything else: both hands are busy, and both are buttery. Phones stay in pockets. Conversation, which at most meals is squeezed into the gaps between forkfuls, becomes the main business of the table, and the growing heap of leaves becomes a kind of clock. It is the best twenty minutes in any week I know.

My grandfather, who on other days ate as if someone might take his plate, worked through his artichoke leaf by leaf and told long stories as he went, about the farm he grew up on and the men he had worked beside. He timed them, I think, to the leaves. By the time he reached the heart the story was over, and he would cut the heart into quarters and pass them to the rest of us.

Restaurants have tried to spare diners all this. They serve the hearts alone, marinated in jars, or chopped into dips, or grilled in neat halves with the choke already gone. I eat these happily, and they taste nearly as good. But they are a different food. A jar of hearts is a dish; a whole artichoke is an evening. To skip the leaves is to keep the prize and throw away the game that made it one.

In dry summers the main street of Tolliver was less a road than a supply of dust. Every wagon raised a cloud of it, and the merchants along Grand Street swept it from their floors three times a day and wiped it from the glass cases that held their goods. In 1879 a group of them hired a teamster named Owen Kett to drive a sprinkling wagon, a wooden tank on wheels with a pipe full of holes across the back, up and down the street each morning.

The arrangement was private. Each merchant paid Kett by the foot for the frontage he wanted wet, and Kett, who was paid for nothing else, opened his valve in front of subscribers and closed it in front of everyone else. By midsummer Grand Street had become a stripe of mud and dust: dark and settled before the hardware store, pale and blowing before the bakery next door, dark again at the bank.

The bakery belonged to Hattie Moss, a widow who had declined to subscribe. Her reason, which she gave in a letter to the Tolliver Courier, was that dust ignores property lines. The wind lifted it from her dry stretch and laid it on the wet ones, and carried it in from the country road onto all of them. A street wet in patches, she argued, kept no one clean, and paying for one patch made little sense.

The subscribers answered that she was taking a free ride, since their wet frontage settled dust that would otherwise reach her counter. Both claims were partly true, and neither could be settled by argument. That August the council clerk, a surveyor named Rufus Dane, tried measurement instead. On six mornings he set out clean plates of glass at fourteen doorways along the street, wet and dry, and in the evening weighed the dust each had gathered on a druggist's balance.

The plates divided in a way neither side expected. Glass in front of the dry bakery gathered more dust than glass at the wet hardware store, but only about a third more, and the plates at the two ends of the street, where the country road came in, gathered more than any doorway in the middle, wet or dry. Most of Grand Street's dust, Dane concluded, came from beyond it, on the wheels of farm wagons and off the open road.

His report recommended two changes, and the council adopted both the following spring. The sprinkling would be paid from the town's own funds and would cover the whole street, every frontage alike. And Kett would begin each morning on the last two hundred yards of the country road, where the dust started, before he turned onto Grand Street.

Hattie Moss paid her share of the new tax promptly, the Courier noted, and that summer she set a bench outside the bakery. Dane's plates, wrapped in newspaper, are still in a drawer at the county historical society, and the dust on the last of them has never been wiped off.

And Kett would begin each morning on the last two hundred yards of the country road, where the dust started, before he turned onto Grand Street.

Hattie Moss paid her share of the new tax promptly, the Courier noted, and that summer she set a bench outside the bakery. Dane's plates, wrapped in newspaper, are still in a drawer at the county historical society, and the dust on the last of them has never been wiped off.

item.passage:
Across large stretches of the world's deserts, the ground is paved. Stones, most of them smaller than a fist, lie packed edge to edge in a single layer, so closely fitted in places that the surface looks swept. Geologists call this a desert pavement. For much of the twentieth century the usual explanation was that the stones had been left behind. Wind and occasional rain, the reasoning went, carried away the sand and silt from the top of a stony soil, and the stones, too heavy to move, settled together as the ground around them was lowered.

In the 1980s a team of geologists tested that idea on an unusual landscape in the Mojave Desert of California. In the Cima volcanic field, lava flows of very different ages lie near one another, some relatively young and others hundreds of thousands of years old. Each flow began as bare rock, so the team could compare pavements whose starting dates were roughly known.

What they found under the stones fit the old story poorly. Beneath the pavements lay a layer of fine silt with few stones in it, and on the older flows the layer was generally thicker. If the stones had been left behind as fine material was stripped away, the silt should have been the thinnest, most depleted part of the soil. Instead it seemed to be building up. Its makeup also differed from that of the dark lava beneath, which suggested that it had come from somewhere else, carried in on the wind as dust.

The team proposed a different picture. Dust settling on a young lava flow collects in the gaps between broken stones and works its way beneath them. As the silt is wetted and dried, it swells and shrinks, and with each cycle the stones are nudged upward, riding on top of the growing layer. On this view the pavement was never lowered at all. It rose, carried up on the dust that slipped in underneath.

About a decade later, members of the same group added a second line of evidence. Rock at the surface is struck by cosmic rays, which produce tiny amounts of certain rare atoms inside it, and the longer a stone lies exposed, the more of those atoms build up. A stone that had spent most of its history buried and was uncovered only recently should therefore carry less than one that had always been on top. When the researchers measured pavement stones, the amounts suggested they had been exposed for about as long as the lava flows had existed.

The team summed up the result in a phrase: desert pavements are "born at the surface." The phrase leaves room for wind to strip fine material from deserts, as it plainly does in some places. Its claim is narrower and stranger. In at least one well-studied landscape, the stones on top were the first thing there, and the soil grew up underneath them.
